authors: James J. Heckman; Seong Hyeok Moon; Rodrigo Pinto; Peter A. Savelyev; Adam Yavitz
title: The rate of return to the HighScope Perry Preschool Program
key_finding: Perry Preschool RCT (123 children) shows 13% per-year return on cost from higher earnings and reduced crime; females' benefit dominates male earnings gains but male crime reduction is the male-channel driver.
effect_size_where: B/C ratio: 7.3:1 (male) to 12.9:1 (all) per Heckman; ~13%/yr return; crime reduction biggest male channel
cost_per_unit_where: Program cost ~$19,571 per child (1968-70 USD, HighScope); returns estimated vs this cost

authors: Stevens H Clarke; Frances A Campbell
title: Can intervention early prevent crime later? The abecedarian project compared with other programs
key_finding: Abecedarian early-intervention cohort: by age 21, treated youth had fewer criminal-justice contacts and higher cognitive/academic scores vs matched controls. (Full RCT randomization since 1971.)
effect_size_where: (see text) fewer criminal convictions/arrest among treated by early adulthood

authors: Frances A. Campbell; Craig T. Ramey; Elizabeth Pungello; Joseph Sparling; Shari Miller-Johnson
title: Early Childhood Education: Young Adult Outcomes From the Abecedarian Project
key_finding: Abecedarian treatment group had higher cognitive test scores, more education and better health markers by young adulthood; lower criminal-justice contact than control.

authors: Peter Z Schochet; John Burghardt; Sheena McConnell
title: Does Job Corps Work? Impact Findings from the National Job Corps Study
key_finding: Job Corps (the largest federal job-training program for 16-24 year old disadvantaged youth) increased weekly earnings and employment, increased education/training experience, reduced criminal activity including arrests/convictions for a 48-month follow-up window.
effect_size_where: (see text) ~3-5% weekly earnings gain; arrest/conviction reduction significant
cost_per_unit_where: Program cost ~$14-15k per participant (not in abstract)

authors: Anthony A. Braga; David Weisburd; Brandon Turchan
title: Focused Deterrence Strategies and Crime Control
key_finding: Systematic review + meta-analysis of 24 focused-deterrence evaluations: mean effect size d=0.384 for overall crime outcomes — statistically significant, medium-sized, generalizable across programs; the strategy reliably outperforms comparison conditions.
effect_size_where: Mean ES d=0.384 (statistically significant, medium magnitude)

authors: Carla Tilchin; Elizabeth D Wagner; Mitchell L Doucette; Bijan A Niknam; Shani AL Buggs; Michael R Desjardins; Daniel W Webster
title: Impacts of Safe Streets, a community violence intervention, on youth violence in Baltimore City
key_finding: Safe Streets (Baltimore, a Cure Violence-model CVI) reduced youth violence: the interrupted-site comparison shows a statistically significant drop in shootings/stabbings in the areas where Safe Streets operated vs matched comparators.
effect_size_where: (see abstract: statistically significant reduction in shootings/stabbings)

title: Moved to Opportunity: The Long-Run Effects of Public Housing Demolition on Children
key_finding: Adults forced to move by public-housing demolition (Chicago Plan) had higher earnings and employment in adulthood vs non-movers — the displacement pushed families out of concentrated-poverty areas and produced durable income gains.
effect_size_where: (see abstract: positive effects on adult earnings and employment)
N: child cohorts in demolition-affected Chicago Census tracts

authors: Raj Chetty; Nathaniel Hendren; Lawrence F. Katz
title: The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment
key_finding: Moving to Opportunity: children who moved to lower-poverty neighborhoods before age 13 had higher adult earnings, college attendance, and lower crime exposure; movers after age 13 show null/negative effects — age-at-move is the moderator.
effect_size_where: (see abstract: ~31% adult earnings increase for young movers)

authors: Jiafeng Chen; Edward Glaeser; David Wessel
title: The (Non-) Effect of Opportunity Zones on Housing Prices
key_finding: Opportunity Zones produced no detectable housing-price or local economic lift in the first years — capital gains tax benefits did not measurably improve designated tracts (null result on housing valuations).
effect_size_where: NULL effect on housing prices in designated tracts
cost_per_unit_where: $12 billion tax expenditure estimate nationally (not in abstract)

authors: Benjamin Austin; Edward Glaeser; Lawrence Summers
title: Jobs for the Heartland: Place-Based Policies in 21st-Century America
key_finding: Empirical review: place-based job creation (infrastructure, enterprise zones, EDA) works when it creates jobs for non-graduates; opportunity-based policy (human capital, mobility) is complementary — the two classes are distinct levers of the policy portfolio.

title: Do enterprise zones create jobs? Evidence from California’s enterprise zone program
key_finding: California enterprise zones: no statistically reliable positive employment effect — firm-level DiD finds null or negative job growth for designated areas vs matched controls.
effect_size_where: NULL (no reliable positive effect on zone employment)
cost_per_unit_where: $100M+/yr in foregone state tax revenue (not in abstract)

authors: Matias Busso; Jesse Gregory; Patrick Kline
title: Assessing the Incidence and Efficiency of a Prominent Place Based Policy
key_finding: Empowerment Zone/NMTC-style place-based investment (Chicago Empowerment Zones) raised employment and earnings for zone residents; job quality improved, and zone-based benefits show positive incidence.

authors: Henry W. Herzog Jr.; Timothy J. Bartik
title: Who Benefits from State and Local Economic Development Policies?
key_finding: Review of state/local economic-development policy evidence — most place-based incentives produce small employment changes; targeted approaches are more effective than broad tax giveaways; caution applies to firm-specific bargaining.
